passage: Pranav here. I work in the same design team as Ishita, so I have watched this for months. Our manager always hands the new client pitches to Meera and asks her opinion first in reviews. Ishita's mockups get "fine, ship it." Last Thursday she stayed until eight and put a one-page summary of her project results on the shared drive, time saved and revisions cut, then mentioned it in the team update. After that she asked the manager what the criteria were for leading a pitch. The manager said "let's talk about it" and looked at the clock. Ishita went back to her desk, her mouth a thin line. I don't know if she felt small or just tired, but over lunch she told me she is giving it until the year-end review before she decides about moving on.

qa.q: What did Ishita put on the shared drive?
qa.a: A one-page summary of her project results, showing time saved and revisions cut.

qa.q: What does the thin line of Ishita's mouth suggest?
qa.a: She may feel let down or overlooked after the vague reply, though Pranav cannot be certain.

qa.q: What could Ishita do before the year-end review?
qa.a: Keep making her results visible and ask again, in writing, for clear criteria.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen the question about criteria?
qa.a: The manager may have been caught off guard, since they answered "let's talk about it" and glanced at the clock.

grounding: A colleague observes a worker who feels overlooked under a favouring manager making results visible, asking for criteria and considering moving on.

passage:
Bidisha: T, can I vent for a sec
Tanuja: always
Bidisha: Mr. Sen just gave Ronit the Singapore client. again. third big client this year
Bidisha: they go for drinks every Friday. I don't drink, I go home to Ma
Bidisha: I feel so small. like I'm invisible in meetings 😔
Tanuja: ugh. that's really unfair. I'm sorry
Tanuja: ok, practical question. is there anything in your control here?
Bidisha: my work is good. but no one sees it
Tanuja: then make it seen. send Mr. Sen a monthly summary of your results?
Bidisha: that feels like bragging
Tanuja: it's information. and ask him directly what criteria he uses for big clients
Bidisha: and if it's just "Ronit's my buddy"?
Tanuja: then you know it won't change. and you start looking elsewhere, calmly
Bidisha: ok. summary on Monday, and I'll ask for a 1:1 🙏
Tanuja: proud of you ❤️

qa.q: How many big clients has Ronit been given this year?
qa.a: Ronit has been given three big clients this year.

qa.q: How does Bidisha feel about being passed over?
qa.a: Bidisha feels small, overlooked and invisible in meetings.

qa.q: What plan does Bidisha agree to, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Sending a monthly results summary and asking Mr. Sen for clear criteria, while being ready to move on if the favouritism is fixed, keeps Bidisha focused on what can be controlled.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Bidisha's situation?
qa.a: Tanuja sees it as genuinely unfair, but helps Bidisha look for practical steps rather than just venting.

grounding: A chat shows a young employee whose manager clearly favours a colleague, feeling overlooked and small, who makes their results visible, asks for clear criteria and considers moving on.

passage:
At the sugar mill office in Kolhapur, the manager, Patil saheb, called Thomas "my right hand" and gave him every trip to the head office in Pune. Akash, who had joined the same year and had better audit results, got the filing.

Akash felt it every morning at the tea break, when Patil saheb laughed at Thomas's jokes and didn't look up at his. He felt small, like a spare part.

For a month he sulked. Then he made a list. What could he control? His audit results. How visible they were. Whether he asked.

He started sending Patil saheb a short note each Friday: what he'd found, what it saved. After six weeks he asked for a meeting. "Saheb, what does someone need to show to get the Pune trips?"

Patil saheb shifted in his chair. "Experience," he said vaguely.

Akash went home and quietly updated his resume. He would keep doing good work here. But he wasn't going to wait forever.

qa.q: Where did Thomas get to go on every trip?
qa.a: He went on every trip to the head office in Pune.

qa.q: How did Akash feel at the tea breaks?
qa.a: Akash felt small and overlooked, like a spare part.

qa.q: What steps did Akash take to handle the favouritism?
qa.a: He focused on what he could control, made his results visible with weekly notes, asked directly for criteria, and began preparing to move on when the answer was vague.

qa.q: How might Thomas see the situation?
qa.a: Thomas may simply enjoy the manager's trust and not realise how unfairly the trips are shared.

grounding: The passage shows a young man whose manager clearly favours a colleague, feeling overlooked and small, who makes his results visible, asks for criteria and prepares to move on.
